topics: 🤐 Speech vs. Action — why blasphemy and conspiring witnesses are exempt from a sin offering despite speaking
🐑 One Animal or Three? — Rabbi Yishmael and the Rabbis dispute lashes for eating the fat of ox, sheep, and goat
🔄 Why All Three Must Be Written — Rabbi Ḥanina's proof that ox, sheep, and goat cannot be derived from one another
🍲 Two Offerings in One Lapse — when eating forbidden fat from 'two categories' still yields two sin offerings
🩸 Counting Blood's Prohibitions — Rava tallies the Torah's three mentions of karet and five prohibitions for blood

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Forbidden Fat and the Grammar of Multiple Liability
overview.subtitle: Keritot 4a–4b
overview.hebrewSource: כׇּל חֵלֶב שׁוֹר וְכֶשֶׂב וָעֵז לֹא תֹאכֵלוּ
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf closes out the discussion of what counts as an 'action' for liability (distinguishing blasphemy and conspiring witnesses, whose transgressions are of the heart or of sight rather than of the hand), then turns to the prohibition against eating forbidden fat (chelev). A baraita records a dispute between Rabbi Yishmael, who holds one is flogged separately for the fat of an ox, a sheep, and a goat, and the Rabbis, who hold one set of lashes suffices for all three eaten together. The Gemara works through several proposed readings of why the verse names all three animals, using the hermeneutical principle that 'a matter is derived from its context' to link the fat prohibition to the sacrificial context. It then examines when eating forbidden fat from 'two categories' in one lapse of awareness yields two sin offerings, and closes with Rava's careful count of how many separate prohibitions and karet penalties the Torah attaches to consuming blood.

slides.title: 🤐 Speech vs. Action
slides.subtitle: Why does the twisted lip of a blasphemer not count as an action, while ordinary speech does?

lines.speaker: Challenge
lines.text: If the twisting of one's lips generally counts as an action, shouldn't it count for the blasphemer too, making him liable to a sin offering?

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: Blasphemy is different — it is essentially a matter of the heart. The transgression is the sentiment expressed, not the mechanics of speech.

lines.speaker: R' Zeira
lines.text: Objects from conspiring witnesses (עֵדִים זוֹמְמִין): a baraita exempts them from a sin offering as having 'no action' — yet the verse says 'at the mouth of two witnesses' (Deut. 17:6), meaning they transgress by speaking!

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: Conspiring witnesses are also different — their transgression is essentially a matter of sight (what they falsely claimed to have seen), not the act of speaking it.

callout.label: Pattern:
callout.text: Both exemptions share a logic: liability for a sin offering requires a genuine physical act, and the Gemara looks past the surface mechanics (lips moving) to what the transgression actually consists of.

slides.title: 🐑 One Animal or Three? Lashes for Forbidden Fat
slides.subtitle: Leviticus 7:23: 'You shall eat no fat of ox, or sheep, or goat' — why name all three?

boxes.title: Rabbi Yishmael
items: One who eats the fat of all three in one lapse is flogged three times
The extra names 'ox, sheep, goat' are superfluous unless meant to separate the prohibitions
Yet concedes (Rabbi Ḥanina): for a sin offering, only one is brought — this prohibition is not like forbidden relations, where each verse is fully separate

boxes.title: The Rabbis
items: One who eats the fat of all three in one lapse is flogged only once
The names are needed to exclude the fat of undomesticated animals and birds, learned from context ('a matter is derived from its context') linking chelev to sacrificial animals
Multiple lashes are ultimately derived instead from the parallel karet verse (Lev. 7:25), which does separate the sin offering

callout.label: The real fault-line:
callout.text: Rabbi Yishmael derives the halakha of a standard prohibition from a karet verse; the Rabbis do not — they only derive one prohibition's halakha from another.

slides.title: 🔄 Why All Three Animals Must Be Written
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Ḥanina's proof, applied both to lashes and to the sacrificial 'portions burned on the altar' (eimurim)

steps.content: 1️⃣ Could the Torah write only 'ox' and derive sheep and goat? No — one could object: ox is unique in having more wine libations
2️⃣ Could it write only 'sheep'? No — sheep is unique in its tail being burned on the altar
3️⃣ Could it write only 'goat'? No — goat is unique in its greater role in idolatry sin offerings
4️⃣ Could it write any two and derive the third? No — each pair still has a unique feature the third lacks (fitness for the Paschal offering, idolatry offerings, or altar libations)

callout.label: Conclusion:
callout.text: Since no animal's law can be derived from the others, the Torah had to state all three explicitly — and Rabbi Yishmael reads that explicit repetition as teaching separate liability.

slides.title: 🍲 Two Offerings for Two Categories in One Lapse
slides.subtitle: A baraita: eating forbidden fat from 'two categories' (שְׁתֵּי שֵׁמוֹת) in one lapse still brings two sin offerings

nodes.content: ❓ Rami bar Ḥama to Rav Ḥisda: separate lapses of awareness normally divide liability — but how can 'two categories in ONE lapse' still yield two offerings?
💡 Rav Ḥisda: he ate chelev that was also notar (leftover offering meat) — liable for both chelev and notar
⚠️ Rami bar Ḥama objects: then he should also be liable for eating sacrificial food (a guilt offering for me'ila)!
🔁 Rav Sheshet retries: he ate chelev of a consecrated animal — per Rabbi Yehuda's view of two chelev prohibitions. But Rabbi Yehuda himself concedes only one sin offering applies there!
✅ Reish Lakish (name of bar Ta'utni): he ate the two fats from two separate dishes — per Rabbi Yehoshua, different dishes divide liability even within one lapse

callout.label: Resolution:
callout.text: Only the 'two dishes' answer survives scrutiny — a purely technical, not substantive, division of the act of eating.

slides.title: 🩸 Counting Blood's Prohibitions
slides.subtitle: Rava's tallies of how many separate verses the Torah devotes to blood
rows: Blood of non-sacred animals (chullin); blood of sacrificial animals (kodashim); blood of covering (dam kisui) — revised from an initial version naming 'blood of exudate'
Blood of chullin; blood of kodashim; blood of covering; blood remaining in the limbs (dam eivarim); blood of exudate (dam hatamtzit)
Holds blood of exudate also carries karet, since 'any manner of blood' (Lev. 17:10) includes it explicitly

Just as forbidden fat is discrete from meat (does not combine to an olive-bulk with permitted meat), so blood is discrete from meat — except creeping animals, whose blood does combine with their flesh

callout.label: Method:
callout.text: Rava treats each distinct verse as a distinct halakha to be accounted for — none is superfluous, each teaches its own scope of the prohibition.

summary.principle: Liability for a sin offering or lashes depends on precise textual analysis: whether an act is truly 'an action,' whether a verse's extra words separate one prohibition into many, and whether two lapses or two objects can be shown to divide liability.

flowSteps.content: 🤐 Blasphemy and conspiring witnesses are exempt — their transgressions are of heart or sight, not action
🐑 Debate: does 'ox, sheep, goat' in the chelev verse create separate liability, or just exclude wild animals?
🔄 Rabbi Ḥanina proves no one animal's law is derivable from the others — all three names are necessary

columns.content: 🍲 Two sin offerings in one lapse only works for two separate dishes, not overlapping prohibitions
🩸 Rava: 3 karet verses and 5 total prohibitions map the full scope of the blood prohibition

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: every repeated word or extra verse in the Torah's prohibitions is read as legislating a distinct liability

quiz.q: According to Rava, why is a blasphemer not liable to a sin offering despite speaking words?
o: Because blasphemy carries no punishment at all
Because blasphemy is essentially a matter of the heart, not a physical action
Because he must first be given a formal warning
Because only priests can be liable for blasphemy
quiz.e: Rava explains that blasphemy's transgression lies in the sentiment/intent behind the words — a matter of the heart — rather than in a genuine physical action, so no sin offering applies to its unwitting violation.

quiz.q: What is the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and the Rabbis regarding one who eats the forbidden fat of an ox, a sheep, and a goat in one lapse of awareness?
o: Whether he is liable at all
Whether he receives one set of lashes or three separate sets, one for each animal
Whether he must bring an offering or receive lashes
Whether the prohibition applies only to firstborn animals
quiz.e: Rabbi Yishmael holds the repeated animal names in Leviticus 7:23 separate the prohibition, making one liable to three sets of lashes; the Rabbis hold one set of lashes suffices for eating all three fats together.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Ḥanina's proof, why does the Torah need to write all three animals — ox, sheep, and goat — rather than deriving one from the others?
o: Because Hebrew grammar requires repetition
Because each animal has some unique feature that would let a derivation from the others be refuted
Because the three animals were sacrificed on different days
Because only ox and sheep are kosher
quiz.e: Rabbi Ḥanina shows that any attempt to derive one animal's law from the other two can be refuted by pointing to a unique halakhic feature of the missing animal (e.g., the sheep's tail, the goat's role in idolatry offerings), so all three must be stated explicitly.

quiz.q: How does Reish Lakish (in the name of bar Ta'utni) ultimately explain a case where eating forbidden fat from 'two categories' in one lapse of awareness yields two sin offerings?
o: The two fats were eaten on two different days
The two fats were eaten from two separate dishes, which divide liability per Rabbi Yehoshua
One fat was consecrated and one was not
He rejects the baraita as unreliable
quiz.e: Reish Lakish explains that eating the two fats from two separate dishes divides the act of eating into two, per Rabbi Yehoshua's view that different dishes create separate liability even within a single lapse of awareness.

quiz.q: According to Rava's final count, how many distinct Torah prohibitions apply to the consumption of blood?
o: Two
Three
Five
Seven
quiz.e: Rava counts five separate prohibitions concerning blood: the blood of non-sacred animals, of sacrificial animals, of covering, of blood remaining in the limbs, and of exudate.
